strengths: The paper identifies and formally defines a genuinely underexplored problem — 3D reconstruction of multi-period scenes with coupled, discontinuous geometry and appearance changes — which is distinct from both static in-the-wild capture and continuous dynamic video settings.

ChronoGS builds on the well-founded Scaffold-GS anchor representation, and the proposed mechanisms are sensible and clearly motivated: a one-hot/interpolated period encoding (Eq. 1), base vs. locally period-varying vs. globally period-varying feature decomposition, fixed per-anchor Gaussian offsets, and a geometry activation mechanism that deactivates anchors whose decoded opacity falls below zero, allowing the unified scaffold to express period-specific geometry while remaining a shared structure.

The introduced ChronoScene dataset is a substantial contribution in itself: 8,891 images across 12 scenes (6 real, 6 synthetic based on MatrixCity), with multi-period captures registered in a common world frame, per-period point clouds, and controlled synthetic geometry/appearance changes. Detailed statistics and spatial-temporal point cloud visualizations are provided in the supplementary, and the data is stated to be publicly released.

Quantitative results (Table 1) show consistent best performance on nearly all metrics across both real and synthetic scenes against representative baselines spanning static (3DGS), structured static (Scaffold-GS), in-the-wild (GS-W), and dynamic (4DGS, realtime4DGS) paradigms, while maintaining a compact memory footprint (0.52GB avg vs. 1.16GB for per-period 3DGS).

The ablation study (Table 3, Fig. 8) is thorough, isolating the contribution of each feature type (base, local varying, global varying), and additional supplementary ablations on feature dimensions and initialization strategies support the design choices.

The comparison against per-period independent training (Table 2) is a valuable analysis, showing that joint multi-period optimization improves quality while reducing training iterations and storage, demonstrating a cross-period benefit beyond simply handling changes.

Qualitative results, including temporal interpolation at a fixed viewpoint (Fig. 7), illustrate that the method cleanly switches between periods rather than hallucinating intermediate structures like dynamic baselines.

The manuscript is generally clearly written, with a well-organized method section and a comprehensive supplementary that improves reproducibility (architecture details, training schedules, learning rates, growth/pruning thresholds).
weaknesses: All quantitative evaluation is conducted exclusively on the authors' own newly introduced dataset. There is no external benchmark or comparison to community-standard data, so the evaluation protocol and dataset construction are not independently verifiable; the reported gains rest entirely on the authors' own curation and test splits.

The core method is a relatively incremental extension of Scaffold-GS: adding period embeddings to modulate anchor features, similar in spirit to NeRF-W-style appearance/transient decomposition applied to anchors. The technical novelty of individual components is moderate; the main novelty lies in problem formulation and the dataset.

Claims of 'more accurate geometry' are not directly substantiated by any geometric evaluation metric (e.g., depth error, mesh accuracy against the synthetic scenes where ground-truth geometry is known). Geometry quality is supported only by PSNR/LPIIPS and visual comparisons, which is a notable gap given that geometry disentanglement is a central claim.

The geometry activation mechanism (excluding Gaussians with opacity below zero from both compositing and gradient backpropagation) introduces a hard, non-smooth threshold; the paper does not analyze stability of this discretization, potential training artifacts at activation boundaries, or sensitivity to the threshold.

Temporal interpolation (Fig. 7) is evaluated only qualitatively; there is no quantitative protocol (e.g., held-out synthetic intermediate periods) to validate that intermediate renderings are 'plausible' rather than arbitrary.

Details on the real data registration across periods (GPS priors plus 'human-in-the-loop refinement') are brief; cross-period misregistration error is not quantified, which could affect both training quality and the fairness of baseline comparisons on real scenes.

Some baselines may be somewhat disadvantaged: in-the-wild methods (GS-W) and continuous dynamic methods (4DGS) were designed for different assumptions, and no strong alternative for this setting (e.g., per-period Scaffold-GS with a shared anchor set, or GaussianUpdate [29] adapted to full multi-period training) is compared on the full benchmark; Table 2 covers per-period Scaffold-GS only on a single scene.

Minor presentation issues remain, e.g., typos ('storge cost', 'ascors periods', 'LPIIPS') and some figures with small text; a few claims (e.g., 'first work to formally address' multi-period scenes) would benefit from more careful hedging given closely related works on changing environments (e.g., GaussianUpdate).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically relevant problem: reconstruction of scenes captured across long, discontinuous time gaps (months to years) where both geometry and appearance change, which is distinct from static in-the-wild methods and continuous-dynamics 4D methods.

The ChronoScene benchmark (8,891 images, 12 scenes, 42 sub-scenes, 3-4 periods each, both real aerial captures and controlled Matrix-City-based synthetic scenes with known temporal edits) is a substantial and reusable contribution; the supplementary provides thorough statistics and point-cloud distribution analyses.

The proposed representation is reasonable and well-motivated: a unified anchor scaffold of union geometry with a period-invariant base feature, per-anchor period-varying feature pools, and a global period-varying feature, combined with an opacity-based geometry activation mechanism to suppress anchors inactive in a given period.

Experimental support is relatively comprehensive: quantitative comparisons against static (3DGS, Scaffold-GS), in-the-wild (GS-W), and dynamic (4DGS, realtime4DGS) baselines across all 12 scenes (Table 1), a comparison with per-period independent training showing memory/iteration benefits of joint training (Table 2), qualitative comparisons, and extensive ablations on components and hyperparameters (Tables 3-7, Fig. 8).
The method is memory-efficient (0.52GB avg vs 2.35GB for realtime4DGS) and improves over all baselines on every scene, suggesting the design works as intended even if gains are sometimes moderate.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is modest. The method is essentially Scaffold-GS with (i) a one-hot period encoding replacing time, (ii) per-anchor feature pools indexed by period, and (iii) a hard gating trick that deactivates Gaussians whose decoded opacity is negative (enabled by using tanh on opacity, which is otherwise unphysical). Each ingredient is a fairly direct adaptation of existing ideas; the 'geometry activation' is a simple thresholding heuristic.

The headline claim of 'disentangling invariants and changes' is not quantitatively validated. There is no metric or analysis demonstrating that the base feature, period-varying features, and global feature actually learn invariant vs. varying factors; the ablations only show that removing components degrades PSNR/SSIM, which does not establish disentanglement.

Evaluation is entirely on the authors' self-introduced dataset, which also was registered with 'GPS priors followed by human-in-the-loop refinement.' Since both data curation and evaluation protocol are controlled by the authors, potential registration biases favoring the proposed representation cannot be ruled out, and no external or standardized comparison is possible.

The temporal interpolation capability (Fig. 7, Eq. 1) is conceptually shaky for a problem the authors themselves define as discontinuous: linearly interpolating one-hot embeddings between periods yields 'intermediate states' whose physical meaning is unclear for construction/demolition events. The claim that the model 'synthesizes plausible intermediate states' is only shown qualitatively at one viewpoint.

The geometry activation mechanism has a stated internal tension: Gaussians with opacity below zero are 'excluded from both compositing and gradient backpropagation,' yet the paper simultaneously claims the scaffold 'remains differentiable for regions that continuously evolve.' The hard, non-differentiable gating and its interplay with anchor growth/pruning are not analyzed.

Some relevant baselines appear missing: GaussianUpdate [29], which explicitly addresses changing environments, and Dynamics-3DGS [15], are cited but not compared against, and no justification is given for their exclusion.

Quantitative gains on real scenes are sometimes modest (e.g., avg PSNR 22.16 vs 20.91 for realtime4DGS), and per-scene margins vary; the significance of the improvement is not accompanied by any statistical analysis or runtime comparisons.

Writing contains numerous typos and imprecisions that detract from polish (e.g., 'acors', 'storge', 'temporarilly', 'appperance'), and the release statement 'Our code and the ChronoScene dataset are publicly available at' is truncated, with no concrete URL, license, or maintenance plan given in the manuscript.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored problem setting — 3D reconstruction of multi-period scenes with discontinuous geometric and appearance evolution — and clearly motivates why existing static, in-the-wild, and dynamic methods are ill-suited to it.

The ChronoScene dataset is a concrete and valuable artifact: 8,891 images across 12 scenes (6 real with 1-3 year gaps, 6 synthetic with controlled edits), registered in a common world coordinate frame in COLMAP format, with per-image period identifiers and released statistics (Tab. 8). This establishes a testbed that did not previously exist.

The method is well-motivated and reasonably simple: a Scaffold-GS-style unified anchor scaffold with period-invariant base features, per-period varying feature pools, a global period feature, one-hot temporal encoding with linear interpolation for intermediate timestamps, and an opacity-based geometry activation mechanism. It extends gracefully rather than over-engineering.

The quantitative results (Tab. 1) show consistent and substantial improvements over representative baselines from all three relevant paradigms (static 3DGS/Scaffold-GS, in-the-wild GS-W, dynamic 4DGS/realtime4DGS) on both real and synthetic data, with a favorable memory footprint.

The evaluation goes beyond headline numbers: Tab. 2 isolates the benefit of joint multi-period training vs. per-period training (comparable quality at ~1/3 the iterations and storage), and the ablations (Tab. 3, Tabs. 4-7) systematically justify each design component, including feature dimensions and initialization. The supplementary provides enough implementation detail (grid size, thresholds, learning rate schedules, training phases) to support reproducibility.
The temporal evolution visualization (Fig. 7) directly demonstrates the claimed ability to switch cleanly between discrete period states, which is the crux of the problem setting.
weaknesses: Missing comparison against the most closely related prior work. NeuSC [12] (Neural Scene Chronology) explicitly targets long-term landmark evolution across captures, and GaussianUpdate [29] addresses changing environments — both are cited and discussed in Sec. 2.3 but neither is evaluated. Given the paper's novelty claim of being 'the first work to formally address' this setting, the absence of these baselines weakens the evidence that ChronoGS is superior to the state of the art rather than merely to misapplied static/dynamic methods.

Evaluation is confined entirely to the authors' own benchmark. Since ChronoScene is new and released by the same authors, there is a self-referential circularity; results on any existing dataset (even adapted, e.g., multi-session landmarks) would strengthen external validity.

Claims of 'more accurate geometry' are not supported by any geometric evaluation. All metrics are image-level (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS); no depth, surface, or point-cloud accuracy metrics are reported, despite geometry disentanglement being a central claim (Sec. 3.2, Fig. 3, Fig. 4).

The 'disentanglement' claim is qualitative only. There is no quantitative measure of how well invariant vs. period-varying components are separated (e.g., anchor activation statistics per period, or behavior of base features across scenes); ablations show each component helps but do not verify the decomposition behaves as described.

The temporal encoding (Eq. 1) is essentially a one-hot per period with linear interpolation; intermediate 'synthesized periods' reduce to linear blending of adjacent period features, which contradicts the stronger framing of 'plausible intermediate states' — Fig. 7 shows the intermediates but the paper does not critically assess whether they are physically meaningful.

Some technical choices are under-justified: the geometry activation relies on decoded opacity falling below zero (opacity MLP uses tanh per the supplement), which is a somewhat brittle hard threshold mechanism; its behavior near the boundary and sensitivity to the threshold are not analyzed. Also, Gaussian position offsets are strictly period-invariant, meaning geometry change is expressed only through visibility — the limits of this assumption (e.g., gradual deformation of a static structure) are not discussed.

Presentation needs polishing: typos ('storge', 'ascorss', 'appearence', 'Renderd', 'Ground Trurh', 'It also take'), an incomplete URL in the abstract where code/dataset release is claimed, and 'N/A' entries for memory/iterations of the proposed method in Tab. 2 that should be reported.

Some baselines may be strawmen: 4DGS is designed for smooth continuous motion and is expected to fail on multi-year gaps; realtime4DGS's 5.5-7.4GB memory footprint seems anomalously high relative to similar methods, raising questions about tuning parity.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: reconstruction of multi-period scenes where both geometry and appearance change discretely between capture sessions, a setting distinct from static, in-the-wild, and continuously dynamic formulations. The observation that multi-period data is 'discrete in periods but shared in major structure' is a clear and useful problem framing.

The ChronoScene dataset is a substantial resource: 8,891 images across 12 scenes (6 real, 6 synthetic), with per-period camera calibration, aligned world coordinates (COLMAP + GPS priors + manual refinement), and explicit per-scene/per-period statistics (Table 8). Capturing coupled geometric and appearance evolution fills a real gap, and release of data, code, and poses supports reproducibility.

The technical design is coherent: a unified Scaffold-GS-style anchor scaffold encoding union geometry, one-hot temporal embeddings with interpolation (Eq. 1), decomposition into base/local/global period-varying features, and an opacity-based geometry activation that deactivates anchors in periods where geometry is absent. The design cleanly handles discontinuous changes without assuming smooth motion.

Experimental support is thorough: 8 baselines spanning static, in-the-wild, continual, and 4D dynamic paradigms (Table 1), a fair evaluation protocol (held-out cameras per period), a direct comparison against per-period independent training (Table 2) showing quality gains with reduced storage/training cost, component ablations (Table 3, Fig. 8), hyperparameter ablations (Tables 4-7), and generalization tests on three external benchmarks (WAT, CL-Splats, NeuSC).

Qualitative results (Figs. 6, 7, 9, 10) convincingly illustrate the failure modes of static (ghosting) and dynamic (hallucinated interpolation) baselines and the clean period-switching behavior of ChronoGS.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is modest. The core contribution is Scaffold-GS augmented with per-period one-hot embeddings modulating three feature groups; each ingredient (anchor scaffolds, per-image/period appearance codes, temporal encodings, feature decomposition) is well established (Scaffold-GS, NeRF-W, NeRF-MS, NeuSC). The 'first work' claim should be softened given NeuSC and continual-learning methods address related settings.

Some mechanisms are heuristic and under-analyzed. The opacity-based geometry activation (excluding Gaussians with decoded opacity below zero) is a non-differentiable threshold trick whose gradient behavior at the boundary and sensitivity to initialization are not analyzed. The interpolation of one-hot embeddings between periods (Eq. 1) has no clear physical semantics for scene evolution, and the claim of 'plausible intermediate states' in Fig. 7 is only visually, not quantitatively, supported.

The central 'disentangling' claim is never validated quantitatively. There is no metric or experiment demonstrating that f_base truly captures invariant structure or that f_var/g(t) capture changes; ablations (Table 3) only show end-task PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS degradation. No geometric evaluation (depth, mesh, or point-cloud accuracy) is provided despite strong geometry claims.

Performance on external benchmarks is mixed: ChronoGS loses to NeuSC on the NeuSC dataset (19.35 vs 21.32 PSNR, Table 11). The explanation that ChronoGS targets a harder setting is plausible but partially relies on the authors' own framing; a variant or configuration of ChronoGS adapted to those benchmarks would strengthen the generalization argument.

The synthetic portion of ChronoScene is manually edited from Matrix City, so its 'changes' are authored rather than naturally evolved; the real data (6 scenes, time gaps of 1-3 years) is limited in diversity, and details such as licensing are deferred. Baseline implementations for the multi-period setting (e.g., how 4DGS handles discrete periods) are described only briefly.

Minor presentation issues: memory is reported as 'N/A' for the proposed method in Table 2 while memory efficiency is claimed as a contribution; several important training details are only in the supplementary; and the paper would benefit from an explicit discussion of limitations (e.g., behavior when period count T is large or unknown at training time).

strengths: The paper targets a genuinely underexplored and practically important problem: reconstruction of scenes captured across discrete, long-interval periods with discontinuous geometric and appearance changes, which falls between static and smoothly-dynamic assumptions of existing methods. The problem framing (Sec. 1-2) and the positioning against static, in-the-wild, continual, and dynamic paradigms is well argued.

A new benchmark, ChronoScene, is released with real (6 scenes, 1-3 year gaps, cross-period registered) and synthetic (Matrix City-based with controlled edits) data, ~8.9k images in a common coordinate frame. Detailed statistics (Tab. 8) and point-cloud projections (Figs. 11-22) support the dataset's credibility, and external evaluations on WAT, CL-Splats, and NeuSC are provided.

Results are consistent: ChronoGS achieves the best PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS on both real and synthetic splits of ChronoScene (Tab. 1) with competitive memory (0.52-0.65GB), and component ablations (Tab. 3) plus supplementary dimension and initialization ablations (Tabs. 4-7) are reasonably thorough. The comparison to per-period independent training (Tab. 2) usefully quantifies the joint-training benefit (comparable quality with ~1/3 the storage and iterations).

The qualitative analyses (Fig. 6 on per-period fidelity, Fig. 7 on discontinuous period switching vs. dynamic baselines' hallucinated interpolation) directly illustrate the claimed advantage over both static and smoothly-dynamic baselines.
weaknesses: Limited technical depth/novelty of the method. The core design is Scaffold-GS augmented with (i) a per-anchor lookup table of T period-varying features and (ii) a one-hot period encoding interpolated between adjacent periods (Eq. 1). For observed periods the temporal modulation degenerates to selecting a per-period feature vector, which is close to simply storing per-period models inside a shared scaffold. The claim of a 'temporally modulated representation' oversells what is essentially a discrete per-period feature index; no mechanism grounds the intermediate-state synthesis in any supervision or physical model, so the Fig. 7 'reasonable intermediate states' claim rests on visuals alone.

The 'disentangling invariants and changes' claim (title, abstract) is not substantiated by any quantitative or qualitative analysis of disentanglement quality. There is no experiment showing that the base feature actually captures invariant structure or that f_var/g(t) isolate period-specific factors; only aggregate rendering metrics are shown.

The geometry model is restrictive: Gaussian center offsets are explicitly period-invariant (Sec. 3.1), so all geometric change must be expressed through opacity-based activation of a static union scaffold (Sec. 3.2). This cannot represent translated/deformed structures, only appearing/disappearing content, and the paper does not analyze when or why this assumption fails. The exclusion of 'opacity below zero' via a tanh head is ad hoc and its effect on gradients (Gaussians excluded from backprop) is not analyzed.

Evaluation is dominated by the authors' own benchmark, where the baselines' absolute PSNRs are suspiciously low (e.g., 3DGS at 18.29 dB, realtime4DGS at 20.91 dB on real scenes), making it hard to rule out registration or protocol issues that disproportionately favor the proposed method. On the only external benchmark with a strong specialized competitor (NeuSC 5Pointz, Tab. 11), ChronoGS loses to NeuSC (19.35 vs 21.32 PSNR), and the explanation ('larger and more challenging solution space') is asserted rather than demonstrated. Critically, the natural strongest baseline - a per-period trained in-the-wild method such as GS-W per period - is never reported; Tab. 2 covers only static per-period baselines on one scene, so the headline gains on ChronoScene may partly reflect weak joint-training baselines rather than the representation itself.

The novelty claim ('first work to reconstruct multi-period scenes within a unified differentiable Gaussian-splatting framework') is overstated given closely related continual/incremental GS works cited in the paper (CL-Splats, GaussianUpdate, NeuSC), differing mainly in the discontinuity assumption rather than the machinery.

Presentation and consistency issues that should have been caught: 'Ground Trurh' (Fig. 8), Table 5's caption mislabels the local feature f_i^var as 'the global feature', supplementary references are renumbered inconsistently with the main text (Scaffold-GS cited as [16] in main, [8] in supplement; Matrix City as [13] vs [10]), and the paper text appears to contain raw LaTeX (Eq. 1-4) with undefined macro labels. These are correctable but reflect insufficient care for a submission claiming a foundation-setting benchmark.
Period boundaries are manually defined assuming 'changes within a period are small' (footnote 1); the paper never tests sensitivity to this assumption, which is central to the problem definition.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated problem setting: multi-period scene reconstruction (discrete, non-continuous geometry/appearance changes) is distinct from both static in-the-wild and continuous dynamic modeling, and the paper positions this gap convincingly against existing paradigms (Sec. 1, 2.3).

Significant dataset contribution: ChronoScene provides 8,891 images across 12 scenes/42 sub-scenes with geo-registered multi-period captures and a controlled synthetic portion, plus per-period image/point-cloud statistics (Table 8) and spatial projections (Figs. 11-22). This is a useful public benchmark for an underexplored problem.

Comprehensive and appropriate baseline selection spanning static (3DGS, Scaffold-GS), in-the-wild (GS-W, NeRF-W), continual (CLNeRF), and dynamic (4DGS, Realtime4DGS) paradigms, with consistent train/test splits and evaluation protocol (Sec. 4.3).

Consistent quantitative wins on the proposed benchmark (Table 1) with a notably smaller memory footprint than per-period static baselines (Table 2: 0.57GB/40k iterations vs. 0.65-4.96GB/120k), and supplementary generalization results on WAT and CL-Splats where ChronoGS clearly outperforms prior methods.

Thorough ablations: main-paper component ablations (Table 3, Fig. 8) plus supplementary studies on feature dimensions (Tables 4-6) and initialization strategies (Table 7), supporting the design choices.
Practical benefit of joint multi-period training is quantified (Table 2, Fig. 4): complementary supervision improves quality while reducing training and storage costs relative to per-period training.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is modest relative to the framing: the method is essentially Scaffold-GS augmented with a one-hot period embedding (Eq. 1), per-period local features, a shared global temporal feature, and an opacity-based gating mechanism. Each ingredient is simple; the contribution is more in combination and problem definition than in a new representational insight.

The central claim of 'disentangling' invariants and changes is asserted but never verified quantitatively. There is no metric or experiment demonstrating that f_base actually captures period-invariant structure or that f_var/g(t) capture period-specific factors (e.g., cross-period feature swap tests, or geometry evaluation on changed vs. static regions).

Geometry quality is claimed throughout ('more accurate geometry', Fig. 3/4) but only image-space metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS) are reported; no depth or geometric evaluation supports the geometry-activation mechanism. The 'opacity below zero excludes the Gaussian' rule (Sec. 3.2) is a heuristic whose behavior is not analyzed (e.g., sensitivity to the gating, failure modes when structures genuinely disappear).

On the external NeuSC benchmark ChronoGS underperforms NeuSC (19.35 vs. 21.32 PSNR, Table 11), and the explanation ('operates in a larger and more challenging solution space') is speculative. The strongest external evidence therefore comes only from WAT/CL-Splats, whose settings are not identical to the multi-period problem; primary evidence rests heavily on the authors' own dataset.

Claims about 'plausible intermediate states' and interpolation (Fig. 7, Sec. 4.4) are qualitative only, with no quantitative protocol for interpolation quality; given Eq. (1) linearly interpolates one-hot embeddings, behavior for intermediate t is essentially arbitrary and may be conflated with the gating mechanism.

Dataset documentation has gaps relevant to reproducibility: cross-period registration error is not characterized or analyzed despite reliance on GPS + manual alignment; licensing and acquisition details are deferred entirely to supplementary material; the code link is promised but not verifiable at review time.

Some reporting inconsistencies weaken the presentation: Table 2 lists 'N/A' for our method's per-period memory/iterations while providing overall values, and the synthetic portion is built on Matrix City, which may limit transfer of conclusions drawn from it to real captures.
